newsitem.title: USA: Stocks drop amid sell-off in technology shares.
newsitem.headline: Stocks drop amid sell-off in technology shares.

text.p: Stocks skidded Monday as a sweeping sell-off in the technology sector cast a pall over the rest of the market.
The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average closed down 49.26 points at 6,806.54, while the Nasdaq Composite index lost 22.37 points to 1,335.34.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 1,319 to 1,156 on active volume of 467 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

Technology stocks were dealt a sharp blow after computer networking giant 3Com Corp., the second largest U.S. maker of networking equipment, warned that its results for the latest quarter would fall short of analysts' estimates.
This triggered a freefall that spread across the sector.
About one-third of the Dow's loss was due to International Business Machines Corp., which fell 6 to 142-3/4.

3Com was Nasdaq's most active issue, tumbling 13-1/2 to 37-1/4 on volume of more than 36 million shares. Cisco Systems Inc., the largest networking equipment company, slid 5-1/8 to 58 on 33 million shares traded.

The sell-off extended a recent slide for major technology companies, a sector that had led the way as the market marched higher but sharply reversed course in the last few weeks as concern about their ever-increasing valuations mounted.
"To see so much movement in the blue chip techs is a sign the market's afraid," said Robert Froehlich, chief investment strategist at Van Kampen American Capital.
"It's a case of people being afraid of a technology sell-off and deciding to ratchet down positions even if they're in them for the long haul," he said.
Analysts said buyers of technology stocks had become more speculative during the latest rally, a factor they said likely contributed to the severity of the decline.

"Trading patterns have shown this money was moving from strong hands to weak hands for several months now," said Harry Laubscher, an analyst at Tucker Anthony. "In many cases it was moving out of the hands of people who held it on the way up."

Laubscher said such patterns -- during which "strong handed" institutional holders edge out of positions to take profits as "weak handed" momentum players pour in -- portend turbulent times because the latecomers are more likely to dump positions on any sign of trouble.
The broad selling pulled down Microsoft Corp., which lost 2-5/8 to 97-3/4 and Intel Corp., off 4-3/4 to 151-5/8. Compaq Computer Corp. shed 5-1/4 to 77-3/8.
Beyond the tech sector, the session was fairly quiet, although some retailers did extend their mini-rally from last week.
"Some money appears to be moving to areas like retailers that have not really participated in the rally," Laubscher said.
Sears, Roebuck & Co. rose 1-5/8 to 53-1/8, Gap Inc. gained 3/4 to 32-3/8 and May Department Stores Inc. climbed 1-5/8 to 47-1/8.

Among individual issues, Westinghouse Electric Corp. edged lower after announcing a $1.55 billion stock acquisition of two Gaylord Entertainment Co. cable television networks: The Nashville Network (TNN) and Country Music Television (CMT).
Westinghouse lost 3/8 to 17-3/8 while Gaylord shares fell 3-1/8 to 22-1/4.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks fell 4.13 to 785.43. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.23 to 587.84.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.45 to 412.35. The average share was down 15 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,542.746 down 40.172 or 0.53 percent.
